name: Hana Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead accessible-room booking software at a tech company, where I am among the best at tracing a room mismatch. I use AI occasionally to understand old code but check the hotel’s current room plan. Teo teaches pottery, our children are grown, and higher lead pay has helped us own a small house and save thirteen months of expenses; many local tech firms exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the hotel-booking team that a small AI shortcut can flag two guests for one accessible room, but a person still has to confirm the actual room. I use AI occasionally to understand old code and check it against the hotel’s room plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead accessible-room booking software at a tech company; I am particularly good at tracing a room mismatch. Teo teaches pottery, our children are grown, and higher lead pay has helped us own a small house with thirteen months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing one disputed room assignment with the hotel manager each Friday. We would save 270 monthly while both incomes hold, and pay for the loose stair rail from this month’s wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our own work and money. An accessible-room icon means little if the doorway is too narrow for the guest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mismatch did you find?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The booking page showed a wide doorway, but the hotel’s room plan showed a step into the bathroom. I stopped that room being offered as accessible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why check with the manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The manager knows which rooms have been altered since the plan was drawn. I ask for a current measurement before changing a guest’s booking.

say: I want **accessible rooms** checked against current measurements.
I use **AI occasionally** for code explanations, then verify plans.
think: I have **thirteen months saved** from higher lead pay and Teo’s pottery classes.
I see **housing secure** with our owned house and thirteen-month reserve.
do: **Review disputed rooms** with hotel manager every Friday.
**Save 270 monthly** while both incomes hold; fix loose stair rail from current wages.
feel: **Calm** about current job and household money.
S0.quote: An accessible-room icon means little if the doorway is too narrow for the guest.
fieldNote: Her **lead skill** turns software disputes into actual room measurements.
The **owned house and reserve** support security with two wages, thirteen months saved and no assumed child help.

steps.text: Review one disputed accessible room with hotel manager every Friday
Save 270 monthly while both wages hold; repair loose stair rail from current pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking booking, checking, writing and coding could reduce the hotel software team. A guest should still reach a named person when the accessible room is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink if the hotel contract pays for one automated reviewer instead of a team. Thirteen months saved gives us room, but I would not call the contract secure without seeing the renewal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my director for the written hotel contract renewal and funded lead hours this month. I’d keep checking measured room disputes while the contract runs, and wait for the renewal before changing jobs; if our hours are cut, I’d search paid local hotel-software vacancies only if wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours but not ready to jump on a rumour. A contract number will tell me more than an AI demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When does the contract renew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hotel has a decision due next spring. I would ask for the date and staffing plan in writing instead of guessing at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn a new AI booking tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might once the hotel shows it works on measured rooms, but I am not enrolling in anything yet. I want the contract facts first.

say: I want **named guest contact** for wrong accessible rooms.
I want **written contract hours** before changing my job.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** at contract renewal.
I have **thirteen months saved**, but no signed renewal yet.
do: **Request written renewal** and funded lead hours from director.
**Keep checking measured rooms** while current contract pays; wait for renewal before changing jobs.
**Search paid hotel software** only if hours are cut and local vacancies cover bills.
feel: **Anxious but measured** about her own contract hours.
S1.quote: A contract number will tell me more than an AI demonstration.
fieldNote: She chooses **contract evidence** before a job change, without claiming new AI learning.
The **local search** begins only if funded lead hours are cut and a bill-covering vacancy exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write booking code and answer hotel guests more cheaply than our team. Robots cleaning rooms and changing beds may follow around 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead developer job could end even with my room knowledge. Thirteen months saved buys time to find another wage, but Teo’s pottery classes alone would not cover all our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written notice of any lead cuts and keep a file of three measured room corrections I can explain to another employer. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local accessibility-software openings only where vacancies exist and wages cover our bills; I would keep the cash reserve for household costs rather than buy hotel equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed about a lost wage, though I could search without immediate panic. A measured doorway is evidence, not a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you manage hotel rooms yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a real paid opening existed and I met its requirements. I know the software, not every duty of a hotel manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a hotel job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would check nearby hotels and software firms first. Teo’s pottery students and our home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach booking code first.
I expect **cleaning robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **lead developer wage** could end.
I know **thirteen months saved** is search time, not income.
do: **Record three measured corrections** and request written lead-cut notice while current role pays.
**Apply for accessibility software** after 2028 loss only if paid local vacancies cover bills.
S2.quote: A measured doorway is evidence, not a job offer.
fieldNote: Her **measured room file** makes current expertise visible without inventing a hotel qualification.
The **local search** needs an actual paid opening and bill-covering wage after displacement.

steps.text: Record three measured corrections and request written lead-cut notice while current job pays
Apply for paid local accessibility-software vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives hotels time to check which accessibility complaints need a person in the room. Robots cleaning rooms may follow around 2034, after booking code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the physical room-audit process while still earning my developer wage, though a booking system does not make me a building inspector. I would need a hotel willing to let a trained access auditor supervise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the hotel and my employer for a paid monthly room-audit visit with a qualified access auditor and the guest’s privacy protected. If both approve and the hotel funds the auditor’s time, I’d practise measuring a doorway and bathroom turn; we would save 250 monthly while both incomes hold, and after 2031 job loss I’d apply for paid local access-audit vacancies only if qualified and wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my coding role but glad to measure a real room. A guest cannot turn a wheelchair with a promise in the booking notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the auditor check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The auditor would check my doorway and bathroom measurements against the relevant standard. We would use an empty room, not a guest’s occupied space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hotel refuses access?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the developer job and not claim I had learned room auditing. I would not enter an occupied room to practise.

say: I want **supervised room audits** before AGI reaches code in 2031.
I expect **cleaning robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I could learn **room measurements** on approved paid time.
I need **qualified auditor supervision** before claiming that skill.
do: **Practise monthly room audit** only with both employers approving paid time, hotel-funded auditor and guest privacy.
**Apply for access-audit vacancies** after 2031 loss only if qualified paid local openings cover bills.
feel: **Anxious but learning** from a measured room.
S3.quote: A guest cannot turn a wheelchair with a promise in the booking notes.
fieldNote: Her **room practice** requires two paid approvals, funded expertise and an empty private space.
A later **audit job** needs qualification, actual paid local vacancies and bill-covering wages.

steps.text: Practise monthly empty-room audit only with both employers approving paid time and hotel-funded qualified auditor
Save 250 monthly while developer pay and pottery income continue
Apply for qualified paid local access-audit vacancies if displaced after 2031 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives hotels time to put real room measurements in their booking systems. Robots cleaning physical rooms may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still choose paid work at 68 and have not verified a retirement amount. Our house and thirteen months saved make the next few years secure, while any future audit position still needs a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep correcting room measurements and save 260 monthly while both incomes hold. I’d request a written retirement-income estimate this year; if the developer job ends after 2036, I’d seek paid local access-audit openings only if qualified and wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about a later job change but secure in the coming years. A real tape measure will always tell me more than a hopeful room label.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you resign for an unpaid training promise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would keep the developer wage while it exists. I would not resign for a visit that is not funded or supervised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help with the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. Teo and I will plan from our wages, savings and verified figures.

I expect **cleaning robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a written figure.
I see **current housing secure** with our house and savings.
do: **Keep correcting measurements** while developer role pays.

feel: **Uneasy later**, secure in the coming years.
S4.quote: A real tape measure will always tell me more than a hopeful room label.
fieldNote: She keeps **retirement timing** tied to a written income figure and actual bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could end before another paid accessibility opening appears. Written notice and a real bill-covering local vacancy would help us use savings deliberately.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a guest can use a room marked accessible on a screen. I would trust the doorway measurement over the booking icon every time.

headlineQuote: I would trust the doorway measurement over the booking icon every time.
portrait: Hana is a **58-year-old software lead** with a master’s degree, higher pay and thirteen months saved.
She and Teo own **a small house** while their grown children live separately.
She **uses AI occasionally** but verifies accessible rooms with measured plans.
She waits for **written contract facts** before changing jobs and requires paid supervised room-audit learning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her lead wage before a paid local accessibility opening appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice** and a real bill-covering local vacancy would help.
